title: Thinking Robots Arcade
intro: Six rounds on rules, learning, detection, voice and navigation. Get them right first try to earn ⭐⭐⭐!

rounds.prompt: What's the key difference between a rule-based and a learned behaviour?
options: A rule-based one follows a human-written exact rule; a learned one follows a pattern discovered from examples
There's no real difference between them
rounds.explain: One is explicit instructions written by a person; the other is a pattern the system worked out itself from data.

rounds.prompt: Why can an unusual example fool a model trained only on typical ones?
options: That kind of example was never part of what the model was trained on, so it has no learned pattern to match it
Unusual examples are always classified correctly, never wrong
rounds.explain: A model's guesses are bounded by its training data — an unfamiliar shape of input is exactly where it's likely to fail.

rounds.prompt: What does a detection's confidence score actually represent?
options: The model's own estimate of how sure it is, not a guarantee
The exact percentage of the object visible in frame
rounds.explain: Confidence is the model's self-reported certainty — real robots typically ignore anything below a threshold as too unreliable.

rounds.prompt: Why does this course distinguish face detection from face identification?
options: Detection finds where a face is; identification determines whose face it is — a separate, more sensitive capability with real privacy implications
Identification is a made-up idea with no real use
rounds.explain: That distinction is exactly why this course pauses on consent and privacy — detecting a face is not the same as recognising a specific person.

rounds.prompt: Match each voice pipeline stage to its job.

pairs.right: What the words mean as a command

rounds.explain: Each stage solves one specific problem, which is exactly why a mishearing (text) and a misunderstanding (intent) are two different kinds of failure.

rounds.prompt: What makes autonomous navigation's 'replan' stage the real test of genuine autonomy?
options: It lets the robot adapt when the world doesn't match its original map, instead of blindly following an outdated plan
It's an optional extra with little practical value
It only runs once, at the very start
rounds.explain: Following a fixed plan in a known room is the easy case — noticing change and adapting is what genuine autonomy actually requires.
